questions.stem: For reactions in dilute solution at a fixed temperature, the units of reaction rate are always mol/(dm³·s). Which statement about rate constants is correct?
options: A zero-order rate constant has the units s⁻¹.
A first-order rate constant has the units mol/(dm³·s).
A first-order rate constant has the units s⁻¹, and a second-order rate constant has the units dm³/(mol·s).
A second-order rate constant has the units mol/(dm³·s).
Every rate constant has the same units as the rate itself, mol/(dm³·s), whatever the order of reaction.
questions.exp: The units of k follow from rate = k[A]ⁿ: k must carry whatever units make both sides mol/(dm³·s), so first order gives s⁻¹ and second order gives dm³/(mol·s). The option assigning mol/(dm³·s) to a first-order constant describes the zero-order case, where k shares the units of the rate.

questions.stem: A drug is removed from the bloodstream by first-order kinetics with a half-life of 4 hours. Starting from an initial dose D, the amount still present 12 hours after administration is:
options: 1/16 of D
1/8 of D
1/6 of D
1/4 of D
1/2 of D
questions.exp: Twelve hours contains three half-lives, and each first-order half-life halves whatever is present, so D → D/2 → D/4 → D/8: one eighth remains. The 1/6 option comes from dividing 1/2 by 3 instead of applying the factor 1/2 three times.

questions.stem: For the reaction A + B → products, kept at constant temperature: doubling [A] while holding [B] constant doubles the rate, and doubling [B] while holding [A] constant increases the rate fourfold. Which statement is correct?
options: The rate equation is rate = k[A][B]², the overall order is three, and k has the units dm⁶/(mol²·s).
The rate equation is rate = k[A][B]², the overall order is three, and k has the units dm³/(mol·s).
The reaction is second order overall, and k has the units dm³/(mol·s).
The reaction is first order overall, and k has the units s⁻¹, because each reactant contributes one power.
The reaction is fourth order overall, because the fourfold increase in the second experiment means the exponent of B is three.
questions.exp: Doubling [A] doubling the rate fixes an exponent of 1 for A, and doubling [B] quadrupling the rate fixes an exponent of 2 for B, so rate = k[A][B]² and the overall order is three. Then k = rate ÷ ([A][B]²), which divides mol/(dm³·s) by (mol/dm³)³ to give dm⁶/(mol²·s); the dm³/(mol·s) option borrows the units of a second-order constant.

questions.stem: The Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) with ΔH = −92 kJ/mol, uses an iron catalyst. Which statement is correct?
options: The catalyst shifts the equilibrium position to the right, increasing the final yield of ammonia.
The catalyst raises the activation energy of the reverse reaction, so ammonia accumulates.
The catalyst makes the reaction more exothermic, which increases the yield at the same temperature.
The catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner, but the equilibrium position and ΔH are unchanged.
The catalyst works by raising the average kinetic energy of the gas molecules, so that more collisions are effective.
questions.exp: A catalyst offers a lower-energy pathway and speeds the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor, so the mixture reaches the same equilibrium composition sooner; it cannot change K, the equilibrium position or ΔH. The shift-to-the-right option fails because yield is fixed by thermodynamics, and the kinetic-energy option describes heating, not catalysis.

questions.stem: Manganese(IV) oxide speeds up the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, and the black powder can be recovered unchanged at the end. The best explanation is that MnO₂:
options: raises the average kinetic energy of the H₂O₂ molecules, so more collisions exceed the activation energy.
shifts the equilibrium of the decomposition towards the products, so the reaction goes faster.
reduces the enthalpy change of the decomposition, which releases more energy to drive the reaction.
is consumed to supply the energy that the reaction needs, which is why a little disappears each time.
provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy and is regenerated during the cycle, so it is not consumed.
questions.exp: A catalyst gives the reaction a new route with a lower activation energy and is regenerated in the process, which is exactly why the same powder can be recovered and reused. The kinetic-energy option fails because raising molecular speed is what heating does, and the recovery of the unchanged solid rules out any claim that MnO₂ is consumed.

questions.stem: A reaction mixture is heated from 25 °C to 55 °C and the rate rises sharply. According to collision theory, the main reason is that:
options: the activation energy of the reaction decreases as the temperature rises.
molecules collide much more often, and this increase in collision frequency alone explains the whole rate rise.
a much larger fraction of molecules now has energy at or above the activation energy, so far more collisions are effective.
the enthalpy change of the reaction becomes more negative at the higher temperature.
faster molecules are more likely to meet in the correct orientation, because high speed corrects the approach angle.
questions.exp: Heating reshapes the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution so that a much larger fraction of molecules exceeds the fixed activation energy, and it is these effective collisions that multiply and drive the sharp rate increase. The activation-energy option fails because Ea is a property of the reaction pathway and does not fall when the mixture is warmed, while collision frequency rises only slightly over such a range.
